description: AI controls an aeroponic-aquaponic system, automating lighting, oxygen pumps, root spraying, and fish feeding. It adjusts light colors to plant growth stages, monitors plant and fish health, tracks pH and TDS, and replenishes tank water automatically. Fish waste provides plant nutrients, while root spraying boosts oxygen and biomass. Users can schedule operations via a mobile app. The system saves water, electricity, and effort.
summary: Bahrain receives 75 mm of rain a year and loses 1,840 mm to evaporation — 24.5 times more lost than gained. Official ministry surveys class only 1.49% of the land as good for agriculture and 31.8% as unsuitable, with irrigated soil at 4–15 dS/m. We use NASA Earth observations to separate land where rotation still works from land that has passed the point where reclamation pays, and we present a working AI-controlled aeroponic aquaponics unit, built and tested by our team, as the bridge that holds production while a field is rehabilitated. Rotation comes first; the unit is for the land that cannot rotate.
details:
What it does. It answers two questions for a field: can rotation still work here, and if not, what happens to the land and to the farmer’s income.

How it works. NASA POWER is queried at the field coordinates (26.07 N, 50.55 E) for temperature, humidity, radiation and precipitation. ECOSTRESS land-surface temperature at 70 m resolution identifies heat-stress windows at farm scale. GPM IMERG rainfall together with POWER evaporative demand quantifies the water gap. NASA POWER radiation sizes the solar array and grow-light schedule. Soil and water salinity, which no satellite resolves at field scale, come from ministry survey data and our own EC measurements.

Three paths. Where soil responds, rotation with nitrogen-fixing crops rebuilds organic matter (under 1% in Bahraini soils) and treated sewage effluent replaces brackish groundwater so salt stops accumulating. Where soil has passed the threshold, the field is rested and rehabilitated through drainage, leaching with TSE, and halophytes such as salicornia that remove salt through harvest offtake. Throughout, a closed soil-free unit holds production and income while that field is out of service.

The threshold is economic, not agronomic: a field is retired from conventional cropping when the seasonal cost of leaching and drainage exceeds the gross margin of its best viable salt-tolerant crop.

Tools and hardware. The aeroponic aquaponics unit uses a solar panel and battery, LED grow lighting, timed misting, and a multi-parameter monitor reading pH, EC, temperature and dissolved oxygen, controlled from a phone application.

Scope and provenance. The hardware unit is prior team work and is presented here as field evidence, not as this hackathon’s output. What we produced during the hackathon is the NASA data mapping, the resolution assessment, and the three-path decision framing above.

Known limits. SMAP’s 36 km footprint exceeds the width of Bahrain’s main island (~16 km), so it informs regional drought context only. The 90% water saving is a design figure from closed-loop reuse, not yet an instrumented measurement; measuring m³/kg against an ET baseline is our next step.
